issues.ko: 뱀은 매 턴 머리를 위·아래·왼쪽·오른쪽 중 한 방향으로 한 칸 움직이고, 몸의 나머지 칸은 각각 바로 앞 칸이 있던 자리로 따라간다. 판 가장자리에서 판 밖 쪽으로 움직이면 죽지 않고 같은 행(또는 같은 열)의 반대쪽 끝 칸으로 나온다. 머리가 벽(#) 칸에 들어가거나, 움직이기 직전에 몸(꼬리 포함)이 있던 칸에 들어가면 죽는다. 머리가 먹이(*) 칸에 들어가면 먹이를 먹고, 그 턴에는 꼬리가 따라오지 않고 제자리에 남아 길이가 1 늘어난다. 먹이는 하나뿐이고 먹은 뒤 새로 생기지 않는다.
issues.en: Each turn, the snake moves its head one cell in one of the directions up, down, left, or right, and each remaining cell of the body follows to the spot where the cell right ahead of it was. If it moves from the edge of the board toward the outside of the board, it does not die but comes out at the cell at the opposite end of the same row (or the same column). If the head enters a wall (#) cell, or enters a cell where the body (including the tail) was just before the move, the snake dies. If the head enters a food (*) cell, the snake eats the food, and on that turn the tail does not follow but stays in place, so the length increases by 1. There is only one piece of food, and no new food appears after it is eaten.
issues.explanation: The Korean sentence has no subject; the topic "뱀은" of the first sentence carries over, so the subject is the snake. In English the nearest antecedent of "it" is "the cell right ahead of it" / "each remaining cell"; naming the snake matches the Korean topic. The sentence exists only in this twin, so the twin pairing is unaffected.
